---
title: "The Millennium Bridge"
subtitle: "Module 2: Synchronization and Collective Behaviour"
format: html
---

The London Millennium Footbridge opened on 10 June 2000. On the opening day it moved sideways, unexpectedly, when crowds crossed it [@dallard2001london]. The engineers found that the lateral force from pedestrians depended on the motion of the deck. They concluded that the same effect could occur on any bridge with a lateral frequency below about 1.3 Hz carrying enough pedestrians. The bridge was retrofitted with viscous and tuned mass dampers [@dallard2001london].

@strogatz2005bridge explained the onset with a Kuramoto-type model. Bridge wobbling and crowd synchrony are two sides of one instability, and both appear when the crowd exceeds a critical size.

## Modelling assumptions

- The bridge is a single lateral vibration mode, a damped harmonic oscillator.
- Each pedestrian is a phase oscillator whose sideways force is periodic in the stepping phase.
- Pedestrians do not interact with each other. They interact only through the bridge.

## Bridge

Let $X(t)$ be the lateral displacement of the relevant mode. With $N$ pedestrians,

$$
M\ddot X + B\dot X + KX = G\sum_{i=1}^N \sin\Theta_i,
\qquad
\Omega_0 = \sqrt{K/M}.
$$ {#eq-bridge}

$M$, $B$ and $K$ are the modal mass, damping and stiffness, and $G$ is the maximum lateral force of one pedestrian [@strogatz2005bridge]. Here $K$ is a stiffness, not the Kuramoto coupling.

## Pedestrians

Pedestrian $i$ has natural stepping frequency $\Omega_i$, drawn from a density $P(\Omega)$. The bridge perturbs the gait according to

$$
\dot\Theta_i = \Omega_i + C A \sin(\Psi - \Theta_i + \alpha),
\qquad i = 1, \dots, N,
$$ {#eq-pedestrian}

where $C$ measures the sensitivity to vibrations and $\alpha$ is a phase lag. The amplitude $A$ and phase $\Psi$ of the bridge are defined by

$$
X = A\sin\Psi, \qquad \dot X = A\,\Omega_0\cos\Psi.
$$ {#eq-amp-phase}

@strogatz2005bridge call @eq-pedestrian hypothetical but testable. It has the same form as the firefly equation in [Phase Locking](phase-locking.qmd), with a stimulus whose strength $CA$ grows with the wobble.

## Feedback loop

Compare @eq-pedestrian with the mean-field Kuramoto equation in [The Order Parameter](order-parameter.qmd). The bridge plays the role of the mean field. Crowd coherence is measured with the usual order parameter

$$
R e^{i\Phi} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N e^{i\Theta_j}.
$$ {#eq-bridge-order}

A small wobble nudges some pedestrians into step. Their forces add coherently and drive the bridge harder, which entrains more pedestrians. For small crowds, $R$ fluctuates at the level $N^{-1/2}$ and the bridge barely moves [@strogatz2005bridge].

## Critical crowd size

For $\alpha = \pi/2$ and $P(\Omega)$ symmetric about $\Omega_0$, @strogatz2005bridge obtain

$$
N_c = \frac{4\zeta}{\pi}\,\frac{K}{G\,C\,P(\Omega_0)},
\qquad \zeta = \frac{B}{\sqrt{4MK}},
$$ {#eq-nc}

where $\zeta$ is the damping ratio. Since $4\zeta K = 2B\sqrt{K/M} = 2B\Omega_0$, the same result reads

$$
N_c = \frac{2B\,\Omega_0}{\pi\,G\,C\,P(\Omega_0)}.
$$ {#eq-nc-b}

Compare with $K_c = 2/(\pi g(0))$ in [Critical Coupling](critical-coupling.qmd). More damping raises the threshold. A narrower spread of gait frequencies (larger $P(\Omega_0)$) lowers it. @strogatz2005bridge estimated $C \approx 16\ \text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ from crowd tests on the bridge. @eckhardt2007modeling analyse the model in more detail.

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise

Check that @eq-nc-b is dimensionless. Use $[G] = \text{N}$, $[B] = \text{kg/s}$, $[C] = \text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ and $[P] = \text{s}$ (a density over angular frequency).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

The numerator $B\Omega_0$ has units $\text{kg}\,\text{s}^{-2}$. The denominator $GCP$ has units $(\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2})(\text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1})(\text{s}) = \text{kg}\,\text{s}^{-2}$. The ratio is dimensionless, as a number of pedestrians should be.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise

Take $P(\Omega)$ normal with mean $\Omega_0$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. Write $N_c$ in terms of $\sigma$. How does $N_c$ change if the damping is doubled?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

$P(\Omega_0) = 1/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma)$, so $N_c = 2\sqrt{2\pi}\,B\,\Omega_0\,\sigma/(\pi G C)$. $N_c$ is proportional to $B$, so doubling the damping doubles the critical crowd size. This is the reasoning behind adding dampers.
:::

You will simulate this model in the graded [Kuramoto Assignment](assignment-kuramoto.qmd).
